items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon / CER claim: How does energy get from a wind farm on a distant ridge to the lights in your classroom?

body.html: Wind turns the turbine blades, and a generator does work on charges, raising their electric potential energy, 𝐸= 𝑞𝛥𝑉. The charges move around a closed loop (a circuit). Transmission lines use very high voltage so that the current is small and the 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 heating in the wires is small. Substations step the voltage down. In the classroom, the charges flow through the lamp (a resistor), where electrical energy becomes light and thermal energy. Charge and energy are conserved at every stage. Claim (sample): Energy travels from the wind farm to the classroom lights as electrical energy carried by moving charges in a complete circuit, at high voltage and low current to limit losses. Evidence (from this module): 𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉 (power carried by a current); 𝑃= 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 (Joule heating loss in wires); a lamp acts as a resistor that changes electrical energy into light and heat.

answer.html: Kinetic energy of the wind becomes mechanical energy of the rotor, and then electrical energy in the generator. Current carries it through wires at high voltage (low current, low 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 loss), substations step the voltage down, and the lamp transforms the electrical energy into light and thermal energy.

items.title: Lesson 1 Focus Question: What parts must a working flashlight circuit contain, and what does each part do?

question.html: A flashlight circuit needs a closed conducting loop. The battery acts as the "charge pump" that raises the electric potential energy of the charges. The bulb lowers it by turning electrical energy into light and thermal energy. The switch opens or closes the loop, and wires connect everything.

answer.html: A battery (energy source), a bulb (device that uses the energy), a switch (control), and connecting wires, all forming one closed conducting path.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (a): Draw a circuit for a toy motor and explain how energy is conserved in it

body.html: In the loop, the battery raises the potential of each coulomb by 𝛥𝑉<sub>source</sub>, and the motor lowers it by the same amount. Charge is conserved, so the net change in potential energy for a charge going all the way around is zero.

answer.html: The battery changes chemical energy into electrical energy (𝑞𝛥𝑉 per charge). The motor changes that electrical energy into kinetic energy (plus a little thermal energy). Total energy is conserved, and a charge that completes the loop has no net change in potential energy.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (b): Why do electricians use schematic diagrams instead of photographs of the wiring?

answer.html: A schematic uses standard simple symbols and straight lines, so it shows the connections clearly and is quick to draw and read. A photograph shows what the parts look like but hides how they are connected.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (c): A student wants the current through a buzzer and the voltage across it. How should each meter be connected?

answer.html: Connect the ammeter in series with the buzzer, so the buzzer's current passes through it. Connect the voltmeter in parallel across the buzzer's two terminals.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (d): A heating coil has a resistance of 24 Ω. What does that tell you?

answer.html: It tells you that 24 V of potential difference is needed for every 1 A of current: 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼= 24 V/A = 24 𝛺. A larger resistance means less current for the same voltage.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (e): A student graphs current versus voltage for a resistor (straight line through the origin) and for a diode (curved, with current in only one direction). Which obeys Ohm's law?

answer.html: The resistor obeys Ohm's law because its 𝐼-𝛥𝑉 graph is a straight line through the origin (constant 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼). The diode does not, because its resistance changes with voltage and direction.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (f): Name two ways to cut the current in a stage lamp circuit to one half

question.html: Since 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅, current changes when 𝛥𝑉 or 𝑅 changes.

answer.html: (1) Reduce the source voltage to one half (if 𝑅 is fixed); (2) double the circuit's resistance, for example by adding a variable resistor (dimmer) in series.

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 9: A potentiometer is in series with a toy fan motor. A student turns the knob to reduce its resistance. What happens to the fan?

answer.html: The total resistance falls, so the current rises (𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅) and the fan speeds up. Raising the resistance would slow it.

items.title: 1 (Lesson 1, Practice): A lantern lamp is connected to a 9.0-V battery and draws 1.4 A. How much power does it use?

body.html: 𝛥𝑉= 9.0 V, 𝐼= 1.4 A. Find 𝑃.
Electrical power is current times potential difference.

answer.html: 𝑃≈13 W

check.html: A lantern lamp of a few watts to a few tens of watts is typical.

items.title: 2: What current does a 40.0-W lightbulb draw from a 115-V outlet?

body.html: 𝑃= 40.0 W, 𝛥𝑉= 115 V. Find 𝐼.
𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉, so 𝐼= 𝑃/ 𝛥𝑉.

check.html: Units: W/V=A . A small bulb draws a fraction of an ampere.

items.title: 3: A halogen lamp that is 100% efficient draws 0.80 A at 110 V. At what rate does it transform electrical energy into light?

body.html: 𝐼= 0.80 A, 𝛥𝑉= 110 V. Find the rate of energy transformation 𝑃.
With 100% efficiency all the electrical power becomes light, so the rate is 𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉.

answer.html: 𝑃= 88 W (88 J of electrical energy becomes light every second)

check.html: 1 W = 1 J/s, and the number is a reasonable lamp size.

items.title: 4: A winch motor draws 150 A from a 24-V supply for 8.0 s. How much electrical energy does it receive?

body.html: 𝐼= 150 A, 𝛥𝑉= 24 V, 𝑡= 8.0 s. Find 𝐸.
𝐸= 𝑃𝑡 and 𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉.

check.html: About 3.6 kW for 8 s is roughly 29 kJ.

items.title: 5: A 48-V generator delivers 2.4 kW. What current does it supply?

body.html: 𝛥𝑉= 48 V, 𝑃= 2.4 kW = 2400 W. Find 𝐼.
𝐼= 𝑃/ 𝛥𝑉.

answer.html: 𝐼= 50 A (to two sig figs, 5.0 × 10<sup>1</sup> A)

check.html: Low voltage with high power needs a large current.

items.title: 6: An LED headlamp uses 0.45 W at 4.5 V. What current does it draw?

body.html: 𝑃= 0.45 W, 𝛥𝑉= 4.5 V. Find 𝐼.

check.html: A headlamp drawing about a tenth of an ampere is realistic.

items.title: 7 (Challenge): The voltage across a pump motor is tripled and its current becomes 2.5 times as large. What happens to the motor's power?

body.html: 𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉, so if 𝛥𝑉→3𝛥𝑉 and 𝐼→2.5𝐼:

answer.html: The motor's power becomes 7.5 times as large.

check.html: Power is proportional to both factors, so the multipliers multiply: 3 × 2.5 = 7.5.

items.title: 8: Draw a circuit diagram with a 48.0-V battery, an ammeter, and a 16.0-Ω resistor in series, with current arrows. What does the ammeter read?

body.html: Put the battery on the left with its positive terminal on top. A wire runs from the + terminal through the ammeter and the resistor and back to the − terminal. Conventional current leaves the + terminal. The ammeter reads 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅= 48.0 / 16.0 = 3.00 A.

answer.html: See diagram: one loop (battery, ammeter, 16.0 Ω) with arrows leaving the + terminal and returning to the − terminal. The ammeter reads 3.00 A.

items.title: 9: Draw a circuit diagram with a 9.0-V battery, a resistor, and an ammeter reading 120 mA. What is the resistor's value?

body.html: Same layout. The resistance follows from Ohm's law: 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼= 9.0 V / 0.120 A = 75 𝛺.

answer.html: See diagram: battery (+ on top), ammeter in series reading 120 mA, resistor of 75 𝛺, with conventional-current arrows out of the + terminal.

items.title: 10: Add a voltmeter across the resistor in each of the two circuits of the previous two problems

body.html: A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component, with its + terminal toward the side nearer the battery's + terminal. With negligible wire resistance, each voltmeter reads the battery voltage.

answer.html: See diagram: a voltmeter V across each resistor. It reads 48.0 V in the first circuit and 9.0 V in the second.

items.title: 11: Draw a circuit with a battery, a small motor, a rheostat (to adjust its speed), and an on-off switch

body.html: Put the rheostat in series with the motor so changing its resistance changes the motor's current, and so its speed. The switch is also in series so opening it breaks the loop.

answer.html: See diagram: battery, switch, motor, and rheostat all in one series loop.

items.title: 12 (Challenge): Add an ammeter and a voltmeter that reads the voltage across the motor

body.html: The ammeter goes in series so the motor's current passes through it. The voltmeter goes in parallel with the motor only.

answer.html: See diagram: the same series loop with an ammeter in series and a voltmeter connected across the motor's two terminals.

items.title: 13: A 47-Ω lamp is connected across a 9.0-V battery. What current flows?

body.html: 𝑅= 47 𝛺, 𝛥𝑉= 9.0 V. Find 𝐼.

check.html: Resistance in ohms is larger than the voltage in volts, so 𝐼< 1 A.

items.title: 14: A light sensor carries 5.0 × 10−5 A when connected to a 4.5-V battery. What is its resistance?

body.html: 𝐼= 5.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> A, 𝛥𝑉= 4.5 V. Find 𝑅.

check.html: A tiny current from a few volts needs a large resistance.

items.title: 15: A motor has a resistance of 45 Ω and carries 2.4 A. What is the source voltage?

body.html: 𝑅= 45 𝛺, 𝐼= 2.4 A. Find 𝛥𝑉.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑉≈1.1 × 10<sup>2</sup> V

check.html: Units A · 𝛺= V; a plausible line voltage.

items.title: 16: A lamp draws 0.80 A from a 115-V line. Find (a) its resistance and (b) its power

body.html: 𝐼= 0.80 A, 𝛥𝑉= 115 V. Find (a) 𝑅, (b) 𝑃.
(a) 𝑅=<sub> </sub><sup>𝛥</sup><sup>𝑉</sup> <sub>𝐼</sub>=<sup> </sup><sup>115</sup><sup> </sup><sup>V</sup> <sub>0.80</sub><sub> </sub><sub>A</sub> = 143.75 𝛺

body.html: 𝑃= 60.0 W, 𝛥𝑉= 110 V. Find (a) 𝐼, (b) 𝑅.

<sub>60.0</sub> = 201.7 𝛺, which agrees.

items.title: 18 (Challenge): A resistor is added in series with the 60.0-W, 110-V lamp so that the current drops to one third of its original value

question.html: Assume the lamp's resistance stays 201.7 𝛺 and the source stays at 110 V.

body.html: Original current 0.5455 A, so the new current is 𝐼′ = 0.5455 / 3 = 0.1818 A. Find (a) the lamp's 𝛥𝑉, (b) the added resistance, (c) the lamp's power.
(a) 𝛥𝑉<sub>lamp</sub> = 𝐼′𝑅<sub>lamp</sub> = (0.1818 A)(201.7 𝛺) = 36.7 V.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑉<sub>lamp</sub> ≈36.7 V (one third of the source voltage) (b) Total resistance needed: 𝑅<sub>tot</sub> = 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼′ = 110 / 0.1818 = 605 𝛺. Added resistance: 605 −201.7 = 403 𝛺.
𝑅<sub>added</sub> ≈4.0 × 10<sup>2</sup> 𝛺 (twice the lamp's own resistance) (c) 𝑃= 𝐼′<sup>2</sup>𝑅<sub>lamp</sub> = (0.1818 A)<sup>2</sup>(201.7 𝛺) = 6.67 W
𝑃≈6.7 W (one ninth of the original 60.0 W)

check.html: One third of the current in a fixed resistance gives (1 / 3)<sup>2</sup> = 1 / 9 of the power: 60.0 / 9 = 6.67 W.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress Problem 19: A charged capacitor and a wire carrying a current both hold electrical energy. Name the form of electrical energy in each

answer.html: The charged capacitor stores energy of position: electric potential energy of separated charges. The current-carrying wire has energy of motion: the kinetic energy of the moving charges.

items.title: 20: Draw a schematic of a battery and a motor that will run

body.html: The motor runs only if there is a complete closed loop from one battery terminal, through the motor, to the other terminal.

answer.html: See diagram: battery, motor and wires forming one complete loop, with no gaps.

items.title: 21: Sam says that if he halves the voltage across a nichrome coil, its resistance will also be halved because 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼. Is he correct?

body.html: 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼 is the definition of resistance. For an ohmic conductor, 𝐼 is proportional to 𝛥𝑉, so halving 𝛥𝑉 halves 𝐼, and the ratio stays the same. Resistance depends on material, length, area and temperature, not on the applied voltage.

answer.html: No. Halving the voltage halves the current, so 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼 is unchanged (for an ohmic conductor).

items.title: 22: A 24-Ω circuit is on an 18-V battery. By how much does the power change if the resistance drops to 20.0 Ω?

body.html: 𝛥𝑉= 18 V, 𝑅<sub>1</sub> = 24 𝛺, 𝑅<sub>2</sub> = 20.0 𝛺. Find 𝛥𝑃.
For a fixed voltage, 𝑃= (𝛥𝑉)<sup>2</sup> / 𝑅.

answer.html: The power increases by 2.7 W (from 13.5 W to 16.2 W).

check.html: Lower resistance at the same voltage gives more current and more power.

items.title: 23: How could you measure the resistance of a coil of wire with a battery, voltmeter and ammeter? If the meters read 1.80 V and 0.250 A, what is 𝑅?

body.html: Use 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼. Put the ammeter in series with the coil and the voltmeter in parallel across the coil.
Close the circuit and read both meters. With the sample readings:
Repeating with several battery voltages and averaging (or using the slope of a 𝛥𝑉 versus 𝐼 graph) improves accuracy.

answer.html: Ammeter in series, voltmeter across the coil, then 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼. For the sample readings, 𝑅= 7.2 𝛺.

items.title: 24: A circuit transforms 4.8 × 103 J in 5.0 min. How much energy does it transform in 2.0 h?

body.html: 𝐸<sub>1</sub> = 4.8 × 10<sup>3</sup> J, 𝑡<sub>1</sub> = 5.0 min = 300 s, 𝑡<sub>2</sub> = 2.0 h = 7200 s.
At a constant rate, 𝐸= 𝑃𝑡.

check.html: 2.0 h is 24 times 5.0 min, and 24 × 4.8 × 10<sup>3</sup> = 1.15 × 10<sup>5</sup>.

items.title: 25: A student says the electrical energy used by a heater "disappears." Where does it go?

answer.html: It does not disappear. The moving electrons collide with the atoms of the heating element and make them vibrate more, so the electrical energy becomes thermal energy, which then spreads into the surroundings. The energy is conserved, but it is spread out among so many particles that it cannot easily be turned back into electrical energy.

items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon / CER claim: How does energy get from the power plant to the lights in your home?

body.html: A generator at the plant does work on charges and raises their electric potential energy, 𝐸= 𝑞𝛥𝑉. The charges move through a closed loop of wires (a circuit). Transmission lines use very high voltage so the current is small and 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 losses are small. Substations step the voltage down. In your home the charges flow through the lamp filament (a resistor), where their electrical potential energy becomes radiant and thermal energy. Charge and energy are both conserved at every stage. Claim (sample, written here): Energy travels from the plant to your lights as electrical energy carried by moving charges in a complete circuit, at high voltage and low current to limit losses. Evidence (from this module): 𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉 (power carried by a current); 𝑃= 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 (Joule heating loss in wires, which is why long-distance lines use high 𝛥𝑉 and small 𝐼); a lamp acts as a resistor that transforms electrical energy to light and heat.

answer.html: Chemical, kinetic or other energy is converted to electrical energy by a generator. Electric current carries it through wires at high voltage (low current, low 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 loss). Substations step the voltage down, and the lamp filament transforms the electrical energy into light and thermal energy.

items.title: Lesson 1 Focus Question: What is an electric circuit?

question.html: An electric circuit is any closed conducting loop that lets charge flow. It contains a "charge pump" (battery or generator) that raises the electric potential energy of charges, and one or more devices (lamp, motor, heater) that lower it by turning electrical energy into other forms.

answer.html: A closed conducting path, containing a source of electrical energy and devices that use it, through which charges can flow continuously.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (a): Draw a circuit and explain how energy is conserved in it

body.html: In a loop, the battery raises the potential of each coulomb by 𝛥𝑉<sub>source</sub>, and the lamp lowers it by the same amount. Charge is conserved, so the net change in potential energy for a charge going all the way around is zero. The circuit is drawn in Check Your Progress 20 below (battery, switch or wire, and lamp in one loop).

answer.html: The battery transforms chemical energy to electrical energy (𝑞𝛥𝑉 per charge). The lamp transforms the same amount of electrical energy into light and thermal energy. Total energy is conserved, with no net change in the charges' energy after a full loop.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (b): How does a schematic compare to an artist's drawing?

answer.html: Both show the same circuit and the same connections. The schematic uses standard simple symbols and straight lines, so it is quicker to draw and read; the drawing shows what the parts actually look like.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (c): What do an ammeter and a voltmeter measure?

answer.html: An ammeter measures the current through a component (connected in series). A voltmeter measures the potential difference across a component (connected in parallel).

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (d): Define resistance in your own words

answer.html: Resistance is how strongly an object opposes current: the potential difference needed per unit of current, 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼, measured in ohms.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (e): Which devices obey Ohm's law?

answer.html: Devices whose resistance stays constant as the voltage (and its direction) changes, such as most metal wires and ordinary resistors over a limited range. Transistors and diodes do not obey Ohm's law.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (f): List two ways to control the current in a simple circuit

question.html: Since 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅, current can be changed by changing 𝛥𝑉 or 𝑅.

answer.html: (1) Change the source voltage 𝛥𝑉; (2) change the resistance 𝑅 (for example with a variable resistor).

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 9: Explain what effect the potentiometer has on the motor

answer.html: The potentiometer is a variable resistor in series with the motor. Increasing its resistance lowers the circuit current (𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅) and slows the motor; decreasing it raises the current and speeds the motor up.

items.title: 1 (Lesson 1, Practice): Lamp across a 12-V car battery, Figure 4. Power used?

body.html: 𝛥𝑉= 12 V; from Figure 4 the current is 𝐼= 2.0 A. Find 𝑃.
Electrical power is current times potential difference.

answer.html: 𝑃= 24 W

check.html: A 12 V automotive lamp of a few tens of watts is typical.

items.title: 2: Current through a 75-W lightbulb on a 125-V outlet

body.html: 𝑃= 75 W, 𝛥𝑉= 125 V. Find 𝐼.
𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉, so 𝐼= 𝑃/ 𝛥𝑉.

check.html: Units: W/V=A . A household bulb draws a fraction of an ampere.

items.title: 3: Rate at which a bulb transforms energy (𝐼= 0.50 A, 125 V, 100% efficient)

body.html: 𝐼= 0.50 A, 𝛥𝑉= 125 V. Find the power (rate of energy transformation).
With 100% efficiency, all electrical power becomes light, so the rate of conversion is 𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉.

check.html: 1 W = 1 J/s, so about 63 J of electrical energy becomes light each second.

items.title: 4: Energy delivered to a starter motor (210 A, 12 V, 10.0 s)

body.html: 𝐼= 210 A, 𝛥𝑉= 12 V, 𝑡= 10.0 s. Find 𝐸.
𝐸= 𝑃𝑡 and 𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉.

check.html: Power is about 2.5 kW for 10 s, so tens of kilojoules is reasonable.

items.title: 5: Current from a 75-V, 3.0-kW generator

body.html: 𝛥𝑉= 75 V, 𝑃= 3.0 kW = 3000 W. Find 𝐼.
𝐼= 𝑃/ 𝛥𝑉.

answer.html: 𝐼= 40 A (to two sig figs, 4.0 × 10<sup>1</sup> A)

check.html: Low voltage with high power needs a large current.

items.title: 6: Flashlight bulb, 0.90 W at 3.0 V

body.html: 𝑃= 0.90 W, 𝛥𝑉= 3.0 V. Find 𝐼.

check.html: Typical flashlight-bulb current is a few tenths of an ampere.

items.title: 7 (Challenge): Motor voltage doubles and the current triples. What happens to the power?

question.html: The wording says "lightbulb" but the question is about the motor's power, so we take the current in question to be the motor's own current (the lightbulb is probably a typo).

body.html: 𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉, so if 𝛥𝑉→2𝛥𝑉 and 𝐼→3𝐼:

answer.html: The motor's power becomes 6 times as large. (If only the voltage doubled and the current stayed the same, the power would only double.)

check.html: Power is proportional to both factors, so the multipliers multiply: 2 × 3 = 6.

items.title: 8: Circuit diagram: 60.0-V battery, ammeter, 12.5-Ω resistor in series, with current arrows

body.html: Follow the book's strategy: battery on the left with the positive terminal on top, a wire from the + terminal to the ammeter and the resistor, then back to the − terminal. Conventional current leaves the + terminal. The expected current is 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅= 60.0 / 12.5 = 4.80 A.

answer.html: See diagram: one loop (battery, ammeter, 12.5 Ω), with arrows pointing out of the + terminal, through the ammeter and resistor, and back to the − terminal. The ammeter would read 4.80 A.

answer.html: See diagram: battery (+ on top), ammeter in series reading 85 mA, resistor of about 53 Ω, with the conventional-current arrows pointing out of the + terminal.

items.title: 10: Add a voltmeter across the resistors of the previous two problems

items.title: 13: Panel lamp, 33 Ω, across the 12-V battery of Figure 10. Current?

body.html: 𝑅= 33 𝛺, 𝛥𝑉= 12 V. Find 𝐼.

items.title: 14: Sensor current 2.0 × 10−4 A from the 3.0-V battery of Figure 11. Resistance?

body.html: 𝐼= 2.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>4</sup> A, 𝛥𝑉= 3.0 V (read from the figure). Find 𝑅.

items.title: 15: Motor, 32 Ω, carrying 3.8 A (Figure 12). Source voltage?

body.html: 𝑅= 32 𝛺, 𝐼= 3.8 A (from the figure). Find 𝛥𝑉.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress Problem 19: Identify two forms in which electrical energy exists

answer.html: (1) Energy of motion: the kinetic energy of the moving charges in a current. (2) Energy of position: the electric potential energy of charges because of their configuration (for example, charges separated across a battery's terminals, 𝑞𝛥𝑉).

items.title: 21: Joe says that since 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼, raising the voltage raises the resistance. Correct?

body.html: 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼 is the definition of resistance. For an ohmic conductor, 𝐼 is proportional to 𝛥𝑉, so doubling 𝛥𝑉 doubles 𝐼 and the ratio does not change. Resistance depends on the material, length, area and temperature, not on the applied voltage.

answer.html: No, Joe is not correct. Raising the voltage raises the current in proportion, so 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼 stays constant for an ohmic conductor.

items.title: 22: A 12-Ω circuit on a 12-V battery. Change in power if the resistance drops to 9.0 Ω?

For a fixed voltage, 𝑃= (𝛥𝑉)<sup>2</sup> / 𝑅.

answer.html: The power increases by 4.0 W (from 12 W to 16 W).

check.html: Lower resistance at the same voltage gives more current and more power.

items.title: 23: Measure the resistance of a long wire with a battery, voltmeter, and ammeter

body.html: Use the definition 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼. Put the ammeter in series with the wire (so it measures the wire's current) and the voltmeter in parallel across the wire (so it measures the wire's potential difference).

Close the circuit, read 𝐼 on the ammeter and 𝛥𝑉 across the wire on the voltmeter, then compute 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼. Repeating with several battery voltages and averaging (or taking the slope of a 𝛥𝑉 versus 𝐼 graph) improves accuracy.

answer.html: Measure the current 𝐼 through the wire (ammeter in series) and the voltage 𝛥𝑉 across it (voltmeter in parallel), then compute 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼.

items.title: 25: In what sense is power "dissipated" in a resistor?

answer.html: The electrical potential energy the charges carry in is spread out as random thermal energy: the moving electrons collide with the resistor's atoms and make them vibrate more, and that thermal energy then flows out into the surroundings. The energy is dispersed among many particles, so it cannot easily be gathered back into useful electrical energy.
